title: Microsoft Fabric Overview: Microsoft Fabric Tutorial Series
summary: An independent tutorial-series overview walking through Fabric's workload lineup, OneLake storage model, compute engines, and a snapshot of platform news as of mid-2026, aimed at readers getting oriented on the whole suite rather than one workload.
audience: Practitioners and architects new to Fabric who want a single-page map of the eight workloads, storage layer, and where recent platform changes (Fabric IQ, OneLake tiers, GPU warehouse) fit before going deeper into any one area.
why_it_matters: Useful as a dated snapshot of platform surface area and recent changes an architect should be aware of when planning around capacity, storage lifecycle, or agentic features, though it is an unvetted community write-up rather than a primary source and should be corroborated against Microsoft Learn before being relied on for specifics.
takeaways: OneLake shortcuts can virtualize data across multiple clouds (not just Azure), which changes how architects think about avoiding data movement/egress.
OneLake is gaining native multi-format support (Delta and Iceberg side by side), which matters for interoperability with non-Fabric lakehouse stacks.
Storage lifecycle tiering is coming to OneLake, but blanket cooling policies risk breaking Delta table reads if applied incorrectly.
Direct Lake's performance promise is conditional — it silently degrades to DirectQuery under several common conditions that teams should monitor for.
The P-SKU to F-SKU capacity migration has firm deadlines that make delaying capacity planning risky for legacy Premium customers.

claims.text: OneLake shortcuts can virtualize data from other clouds' object stores (e.g., S3-compatible and other cloud blob storage) as well as other ADLS Gen2 accounts and Fabric Lakehouses, letting Fabric reference that data without physically copying it.
The post describes OneLake gaining native support for both Delta Lake and Apache Iceberg table formats, enabling bidirectional access with Iceberg-managed tables from other platforms.

The post warns that when OneLake storage-tier lifecycle policies (hot/cool/cold) are introduced, teams must exclude the `_delta_log/` directory from any auto-cooling rule, because the Delta transaction log is read every time a table is opened and moving it to cold storage would hurt performance.

The post lists conditions that cause Direct Lake to silently fall back to DirectQuery: use of unsupported DAX functions, the semantic model exceeding the SKU's memory framing limit, OneSecurity being enabled on the source Lakehouse, and unsupported relationship cardinality.

Per the post, non-EA Power BI Premium (P-SKU) customers reach end-of-life on January 1 2026, while EA customers must migrate by their EA term end or January 1 2028, whichever comes first, with F64 positioned as the functional equivalent of P1.
The post describes a three-phase consequence after the P-SKU migration deadline passes: a 30-day period of free equivalent access, then 90 days of throttled access, then data suspension.

The post states Fabric IQ's Operations Agents, Graph, Planning, and Data Agent components reached general availability together, while the Ontology component (mapping business entities/relationships/rules to OneLake) remained in preview.
The post describes Fabric Data Agent as supporting conversational natural-language queries translated to SQL/DAX/KQL over governed OneLake sources, spanning up to five data sources per agent.

The post reports that Fabric's Data Warehouse engine received GPU-accelerated query processing using NVIDIA compute, characterized as materially faster for reporting and application workloads compared to prior CPU-only execution.

The post describes ADF Mapping Data Flow transformations becoming usable directly inside Dataflow Gen2, positioned as easing migration of existing Azure Data Factory Mapping Data Flow logic into Fabric.
